blocks.text: Verses 11–19 argue that a change in priesthood entails a change in law. The point is not that the law is worthless or that Torah has no continuing Jewish meaning; the chapter contrasts priestly arrangements in order to describe a “better hope” through which people approach God.

Hebrews reads the brief portrayal of Melchizedek alongside Psalm 110 as a literary analogy for Jesus’ enduring priesthood. Thus the statements that Melchizedek is “without father, without mother,” and without an end of life describe how he functions in this textual argument; they do not require the conclusion that the Genesis figure literally lacked parents or was Jesus.

The chapter’s contrast between priesthoods and covenants should not be treated as grounds for contempt toward Judaism, denigration of Torah, or erasure of living Jewish communities. Keeping Melchizedek’s role within Hebrews’ literary argument helps readers avoid turning the passage into a claim of Jewish inferiority.
Christian readings that connect Leviticus with Hebrews are later canonical reception. They should be distinguished from Leviticus itself and its own instructions to Israel.
